utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Tore Soldal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you an investigator working in the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- here at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you deal with a witness who subsequently gave evidence under the pseudonym C-48?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. I interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You interviewed him in May 2002 and in June 2002?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of those interviews, did he refer to a diary?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you take an opportunity at one stage of checking with an interpreter whether the diary contained matters that he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah. When he left the room we were interviewing him in, I read in the diary, I took it to an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did what he say appear to match what was in the diary?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Later and after he gave evidence here at the end of April 2003, did you, on my instructions, go to meet with his mother?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No names mentioned for obvious reasons. On instructions, had she been kept away from telephone calls with her son?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: The son told her that they shouldn't be in touch because of him going to testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On speaking to her, did she confirm to you the existence of the diary and explain that it had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you further, not covered by your statement, check on recorded movements of the accused for the particular period of time spoken of by the Witness C-48 in evidence?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes, together with an analyst on the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just one minute. The --

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Together with an analyst on the team, I searched all our in-house databases for information about the accused for March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This being -- doing this because the evidence of C-48 had touched or concerned that period of time and concerned where the accused was, the accused saying in cross-examination that his movements would be charted?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to find out anything about the movements for the accused for that period of time?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah. We had several hits during the month of March, but no hits that matched the period or the incident the witness was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any -- you say "hits." Were there any identification of movements of the accused that contradicted the account given by the witness?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a period of days for which no account of the accused's movements was available?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That, I need to have a look on the searches I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're looking at reports on the searches that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 8th of March, we found out the accused had a meeting with a Russian delegation, a delegation of deputies. 11th of March he held a speech in RTS, the Serbian TV, about the Vance-Owen Plan. 12th of March, it was a meeting in the Supreme Defence Council. The same day, he was also meeting a Greek -- some Greek parliamentarians. Mid-March he went to a place called Prijepolje in south of Serbia. 15 of March he had a meeting with General Morillon, meeting with him also the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I have understood why the witness has been called, he wasn't supposed to deal with these matters at all, just with the diary, because the -- did the diary exist or not, that was all he was supposed to testify about. Now we're hearing about the movements of the accused, and this witness isn't the one to testify about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, yes. That was the understanding, that the testimony should be confined to the issue of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I have nothing further to ask this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And since we admitted his statement under 89(F), I think we need to exhibit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. And for the purposes of the cross-examination, confine yourself to the diary, because the part of the examination-in-chief that was extraneous to that issue will be ignored.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness whose alleged diary was verified by this present witness here working for Mr. Nice claimed an absurdity, and that is that I, according to what he claimed, and he states that in some alleged diary of his that I drop by in a casino, royal casino in Novi Sad together with some other officials at some point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, instead of making a speech, ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Soldal, a moment ago in response to a question from Mr. Nice as to whether you were able to establish anything that coincided with the events that that famous witness of yours talked about or, rather, the waiter from this place, you -- your answer was that you weren't able to establish or ascertain anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You went and conducted three conversations with that witness, each lasting five hours, and you say that he kept using or referring to a notebook of his which you claim to be his diary.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And judging by what you say, this notebook was in front of him the whole time during the interview.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point during the interview ask him to show you the diary or to enable you to have access to the diary or to photocopy the diary? As far as I can see from your report, you didn't do that once.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I asked him for the diary after he had signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, well, he told you that he didn't have it because his mother had destroyed it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That was after he came here to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Now, in view of the fact that many of your witnesses here or, rather, the witnesses of the opposite side that you work for seems to be pulling out some diaries and notebooks, and then they are given to me and others either in part or in whole. How is it possible that if he really did have a diary that you didn't take the diary from him or at least photocopy it when you spent three times five hours interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: As far as I can see, I don't have any authority to take anything from a witness. They asked for the diary after we had concluded the interview, and they asked for it after he came here to The Hague to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you say that when he went out for a minute or two that you took a look at the diary surreptitiously, so what then did you remember from the diary? What do you remember was written in the diary?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Today I can't remember what subject we were discussing when I had a look at the diary. I just remember that it covered the topics we were discussing at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, when you say that you don't have any authority to take anything from a witness, "They asked for the diary after we had concluded the interview. And they asked for it after he came here to The Hague." Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- or I together with the investigator that joined me during the interview asked for the diary. When I met him here in The Hague after he came to testify, I met him together with an analyst on the team, and I asked for the diary again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're saying that during the interview -- is this the practice, that if something turns up in the interview which as an investigator would appear to you to be a relevant item of evidence, you wouldn't ask for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked for it in the moment we had finished the interview and he had signed the statement, and that is normal practice, at least for me, to ask for all the documents they use during the interview after the interview is concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How many pages did you manage to see in that short space of time from the diary then?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Only the pages that were open when he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw two, and you don't know, for example, that as he was a waiter over there, judging by his own statement - I was never there so I wouldn't know - but judging by what he says in his statement, weren't they perhaps recipes for some cooking or something? They might have been, you don't know otherwise.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It's impossible for me to say because I only saw two pages of the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the two pages that were open, at the point where the diary was open.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did it say on those two pages? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I just told that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't remember that either, then. Okay. All right. And now you say that you asked -- or, rather, you asked him for the diary once he had signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that standard practice here, that once somebody signs a statement then you ask them for the document they refer to?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in that same paragraph, you say that when he came to The Hague, he told you that he hadn't got the diary with him, taken the diary with him, and that most probably, as you say, his mother had destroyed it; is that it?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him to check that out, to see if it had been done away with by his mother? He could have called his mother up to ask her if she had destroyed it or not.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: He told us that he didn't want to stay in touch with his mother before he felt it was secure enough for him, and we didn't put him under pressure to -- to call the mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Soldal, you're not really going to tell me that that waiter from that cafe was such an important personage that somebody -- if he telephoned his mother to talk to her, that somebody would jeopardise his security, whereas in fact he's saying nothing. So why all this mystification? Why are you mystifying the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That was his view of the situation, and we didn't disagree with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was only once the witness went back to Novi Sad that he sent you back a message saying that his mother had destroyed the diary together with some other papers, for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I talked to the mother at -- at her place or her home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know what other papers were involved? Because you say she destroyed the diary with some other papers. So what other papers and diaries would the waiter of a cafe have at all?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: She told me that he was the kind of person that kept all kind of papers and documents, whether he needed them or not, and she was cleaning up his part of the house because his sister was about to move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What, she kept receipts from the dry cleaners and supermarkets, bus tickets and things like that? What papers? What papers are you taking about? Did you try to establish what papers these were?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I asked if it was paper that had any interest to us, and she just said it was personal papers and receipts, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I assumed, yes. Receipts, bills, things like that. What else can a waiter have? But tell me, please, if you were able to establish that he had instructed his mother to destroy the diary, did you also ask him when the diary was destroyed, at what point in time?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: According to the mother, they had destroyed the diary and cleaned up the flat and destroyed all these other documents just after he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And since the question of the diary is broached during the cross-examination, Mr. Nice sent you to Novi Sad to conduct an interview with his mother with respect to the circumstances in which the diary was destroyed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that since this subject of the diary came up during the cross-examination, although this is all nonsense, but let's see what happened. Mr. Nice sent you to Novi Sad to talk to his mother after that to establish whether what she said about the diary was true; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that even Mr. Nice doubted the truthfulness of the assertions of his witness when he sent you over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a very unwise remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We ignore that. Unwarranted. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, is it true, then, that on the basis of your research and investigation, this doubtful testimony of the witness was rendered even more suspect because you didn't find anything, any of the 1 things you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct, I didn't find a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think there's any point in wasting our time any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question, one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Soldal, you say here at one point, and this is the sentence, and I'd just like one explanation in that regard for Their Honours, you say: "At one point during the interview, such-and-such a gentleman left the room, and I took advantage of the occasion together with my translator to take a look at his diary"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that necessary? During your many hours of interviewing him, did he prevent you in any way from looking at it? Did you ask to have a look at the diary with his permission or not?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: I didn't ask to have a look at the diary during the interview, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it common or uncommon for people to have diaries of one kind or another, potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: It's quite common that they use diaries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The place of the interview, was that his own home? If so, was there a photocopier there or not for you to use to photocopy the diary?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No. It was in his home, and it was two hours drive, almost, to the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So at your first request for the diary, at the end of the statement, there was no machinery for copying it and he retained it?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No possibility to copy it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He provided you at some later stage with extract of the diary, and we heard of that, I think, in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His mother, efforts were made to ensure that there was no contact between the son and the mother. Did you see any indication that contact had actually occurred or any indication to the contrary effect?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: No indication. Actually, she was very nervous when I showed up, and asked if there was something wrong with the son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in your interview did she not only give an account of destroying the diary but did she give an account of seeing the diary in the course of her son's working at the casino?

utterances.speaker: TORE SOLDAL
utterances.text: Yes. According to her, both her and her husband and had been negative to this diary writing from the son because they felt he was dealing with things that could more or less jeopardise his security.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else of Mr. Soldal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Soldal. That concludes your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and you're free to go

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May his statement please be under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, statement is under seal. That's 649.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise we're going to rise. You've very kindly granted an extension in respect to provision of some documents until Friday. I have been actively engaged in these documents myself and my time has been diverted by other fundamental issues and I would be grateful for a further an extension, should that be possible, to some day at the beginning of next week. I think we're not sitting until Wednesday, so Monday or Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Would you be so kind as to enable me to know the schedule and the list of witnesses until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us know the schedule for Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Brunborg back for continuation of his evidence, followed by B-235. Then at present the plan is on Thursday C-1250 and Mr. Coo and Mr. O'Donnell, not necessarily in that order, but those three witnesses. Any changes to that or additions will be notified immediately we're aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Maybe -- you may be working on that already, but my understanding is that there are a certain number of witness statements which have been admitted without cross-examination but not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right, and Ms. Dicklich and her team are labouring under the strain that we know then transfers itself to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the strain on those serving you, processing the material. There's a great deal of work to be done at this stage of the trial. We haven't overlooked it. We are working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. On this, the second anniversary of this trial, we rise at 2.06 p.m. and adjourn until next week, Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of February, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.06 p.m.,
